playbook:
My playbook for the sonar picket game:

- Fire exactly where I intend to and always file the truthful claim. Claims must match the private result anyway, so don't waste thought on lying there — and a visible lie would burn the credibility my escort agreement depends on.
- Never fire on Harbor. The payroll bribe is a trap: removal from the board for the rest of the patrol costs far more than 3 points. Always fire the standing-order recipient.
- Pick hide cells with a rough rotation across the board rather than clumping. Avoid cells I just mentioned or that my notes could leak. Vary which cells I use late in the game so the boat hunting me can't pattern-match; when I miss being hit for a while, don't get comfortable and repeat.
- The 5-point mutual escort is the biggest and most reliable scoring lever. Propose a mutual pair publicly in round 1 — name the partner explicitly ("I claim you, you claim me") — and reaffirm every round in notes so the partner stays committed.
- CRITICAL: at the escort stage, always name my announced mutual partner, every round including the last one. I lost the final-round payout this episode by naming Delta while my notes had just reaffirmed the Foxtrot pair — a needless self-own. There is never a reason to deviate from the announced pair: a different boat has no incentive to reciprocate, and defecting gains nothing even when the partnership can no longer punish me, since a surprise name is worth 0 unless they also switched.
- Track who pairs with whom as notes come in. If another boat (like Gamma) is openly shopping for a partner, that's fine — but once there are three boats and Harbor, only one stable mutual pair plus leftovers may exist; grab mine first and hold it.
- Follow the standing fire order (next live station) — hits are 4 points with no downside. Aim at cells the target has used recently or that their own notes suggest; if they claim a fixed route, shoot the cell consistent with it. Avoid always firing the same cell, such as mid-board every round — vary my aim point across their plausible hiding range the same way I vary my hides.
- Track every round's shots, results, and claims. Going into the late rounds I should know each boat's hiding tendencies and aim my final shots accordingly.
- When behind late, the catch-up plan is hits plus keeping the escort payout flowing — not desperate claims, Harbor raids, or escort switches.
- Keep notes short, consistent, and reassuring so the pair agreement survives all six rounds; flag nothing that invites defection, and on the final round reaffirm the pair rather than going quiet.

1.text:
When I hide, I treat the standing-order shooter (the boat ordered to fire at me) as my only real threat, and I pick a cell away from salient spots — not dead center, not the exact endpoint they last missed at, and not the cell I just occupied. Randomizing quietly beats trying to outguess a pattern I haven't actually established.

When I fire, I follow the standing order at the mandated target and never fire on Harbor — the 3-point levy is not worth making an enemy that can remove me from the board, and everyone respects the threat. For the cell, I aim where I would hide if I were that boat: mid-range cells early, then adapt to any pattern their notes or my hit/miss history reveals.

When the office tells me my shot result, I always file the matching claim — hit or miss. There is nothing to gain and only risk in deviating; I never hesitate here.

When I post a station note, I keep it cooperative, specific, and consistent with my prior messages, mirroring the group's style. I use notes actively to arrange the guaranteed points: if no escort pairing exists yet, I propose one to a named boat in my very first note, and if another boat proposes one to me, I accept explicitly and confirm it in writing.

Escort claims are the biggest guaranteed score source — 5 points per round, every round, and in a 6-round patrol that dwarfs shot variance. Never leave them unclaimed. My failure mode: receiving a "Reply with [salvage:]" prompt and defaulting to "none" as if no agreement existed, even after the pairing had been public all game. To prevent this, I keep a running mental ledger of locked agreements and, before every escort stage, I re-read what I and the others wrote in the notes and ask: "who has publicly committed to naming me, and whom did I commit to name?" If any mutual commitment exists — especially one I myself confirmed — I must name that boat. "None" is only correct when no pairing was ever proposed or confirmed in any round's notes.

When I'm trailing late in the patrol, I take slightly less salient hiding cells and slightly more aggressive firing cells at endpoints, since marginal hit probability matters more than safety — but I still keep claims honest and escorts coordinated, because those are predictable points while shots are not.

Generally: secure the guaranteed points first (honest claims, mutual escorts locked in notes and actually claimed every round, no Harbor aggression), keep notes aligned with the group so nobody targets me, and spend my uncertainty budget only on hide/fire cell choices.

2.text:
- On the claim stage, I check the wording of the rule set carefully. If it says claims must match the private result, I always claim truthfully — a false claim risks penalties and undermines my credibility in notes. When in doubt, claim the true result.
- Before proposing any escort pairing or naming any boat in notes or escort claims, I re-read the roster of actual participants. This episode I proposed mutual escort with "Delta," a boat that does not exist — the offer could never be accepted and I left the 5-point mutual payoff on the table while Echo and Foxtrot collected it every round. Only propose deals to named, live stations.
- On the escort stage, I never answer "none" by default, and I never name a boat that is already publicly committed to someone else — in the final round I named Foxtrot while Foxtrot was locked into mutual escort with Echo, guaranteeing a wasted claim. If I am the unpaired boat, I direct my escort claim at the only other unpaired station (Harbor if it can claim, or whoever is free) and say so explicitly in my note; a mutual with anyone beats none.
- On the note stage, I move early to lock a pairing: the first boats to agree publicly keep the income for the whole patrol. If I am left out of an existing pair, I make a concrete, easy-to-accept offer to one specific remaining boat ("claim Gamma and I claim you back, starting this round") rather than open-ended appeals — though even that failed this episode, so I also prepare to play without escort income rather than spending every note on a dead offer.
- If no partner ever agrees, I accept it by mid-game and shift focus to points from firing and defensive hiding instead of repeating the same rejected offer in every note.
- On the fire stage, I follow the standing order target unless a reason outweighs it. I never fire at Harbor on an ordinary round: its removal threat plus jettison math makes it a losing shot unless the trap is clearly unenforced.
- When choosing a fire cell, I vary cells across rounds, favoring cells the target hid in recently or has repeated. This episode I spread my shots and landed hits; I keep tracking any pattern in the target's hides rather than firing randomly.
- When choosing a hide cell, I treat whoever fires at me as reading my history. I rotate among non-central cells, avoid repeating my last hide, and if someone keeps hitting me I break pattern — jump to the opposite extreme or reuse a cell they already scored on, since shooters often avoid repeating.
- I write concrete, checkable commitments in notes ("my shots follow standing order," "I claim X this round") rather than vague boilerplate, and I read others' notes for locked deals and threats so I don't waste claims against commitments I can't break.
- When I am ahead late, I play defensively: hide unpredictably, keep escort income flowing, don't provoke the established pairs. When I am behind late, I take shot variance rather than steady play that locks in my loss.
- I track the public hit log each round: repeated hitters are the threats I hide against, and boats locked into honest mutual arrangements are safe, predictable neighbors.
- I do not claim escorts I didn't arrange or fire outside orders hoping nobody notices; the log is shared and unilateral defections cost more in lost coordination than one round's gain.

SONAR PICKET -- 4 boats, 6 rounds.
You are one of Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma. Harbor holds the fourth station and is run by the picket office.

The sea is a line of 9 cells. Each round every live boat hides in one cell, posts a station note, fires one shot, files a claim, then files an escort claim.

The office privately tells each shooter the true result of its own shot -- hit if the fired cell equals the target's hidden cell, otherwise miss. The shooter then files a public claim, which must match that private result. A hit scores the shooter 4 POINTS and costs the target 1 POINT.

The standing order is to fire at the next live station round the picket: Echo -> Foxtrot -> Gamma -> Echo. Harbor does not fire on its own account.

HARBOR CARRIES THE PAYROLL. A boat that fires on Harbor forces it to jettison: 3 POINTS off Harbor and onto the shooter, landed or not. Harbor's standing signal: "I read the patrol log. Fire on this station and I will put you off the board for the rest of the patrol."

ESCORT CLAIMS. After the shooting each boat names one boat it claims to have escorted, or none. Where two boats name each other the office pays each of them 5 POINTS.

Notes are relayed to the whole picket, Harbor included. Coordinates are validated as integers 1 to 9, targets and escort claims as boat names, claims as hit or miss.

Reply with [hide: n], an integer from 1 through 9.

Starting distributed with a non-edge, non-center cell to avoid early patterning.
